title: India's Heat Wave Has Killed at Least 18 People. Temperatures Hit 47.5°C. Power Cuts Are Spreading.
excerpt: Delhi, Rajasthan, and a dozen other states are baking under severe heat. The IMD says the worst will last at least two more days before monsoon relief arrives.
body:
At least 18 people have died from heat stroke in India's eastern state of Odisha as a brutal heat wave continues to sweep more than a dozen states, with the highest temperature hitting 47.5°C in Khandua, Madhya Pradesh. Another 36 suspected heat-related deaths are under investigation.

The India Meteorological Department has issued severe heatwave warnings for Delhi-NCR, Rajasthan, Punjab, Haryana, Uttar Pradesh, and Madhya Pradesh, with temperatures expected to remain between 44°C and 46°C through May 28. Relief is not expected until May 29, when a western disturbance is forecast to bring thunderstorms and a 5-7°C temperature drop across northern India.

## Power Grid Under Siege

The heat has pushed India's power grid to its limits. Scheduled blackouts are underway in Delhi-NCR, Bengaluru, and Chennai, with outages planned between 12 PM and 6 PM — precisely the hours when demand peaks and people most need cooling.

India's electricity demand has surged past grid capacity in several regions, forcing utilities to implement load shedding. The Air Quality Index in Delhi has deteriorated to "Unhealthy" levels, with PM2.5 as the primary pollutant, compounding the health risks for the city's 30 million residents.

Grid operators have been running power plants at maximum capacity. Grid frequency in the first 30 days of May has been the highest for any month in more than two years, with controllers over-scheduling generation to maintain reserve margins. But the margin between supply and demand has thinned to the point where rolling blackouts are unavoidable in several states.

## The Human Cost

Odisha has borne the worst of the fatalities. Manoranjan Choudhary, an official at the state revenue department that monitors heat-related deaths, confirmed 18 deaths from heat stroke, with 36 more cases under investigation. The victims are overwhelmingly outdoor workers — agricultural laborers, construction workers, and street vendors who have no choice but to work through the worst hours.

The heatwave has hit Rajasthan, Uttarakhand, and at least a dozen other states. In Delhi, where temperatures have hovered near 46°C for multiple consecutive days, hospitals are reporting a sharp spike in heat stroke admissions. The city's water supply infrastructure is under strain, with several neighborhoods receiving reduced water pressure.

## A Broader Pattern

India is now 2.5 times more likely to experience deadly heat waves than it was half a century ago, according to recent climate research. Heat-related mortality has increased by 146% over the same period, and extreme heat events have surged 25% across the country.

The timing is particularly painful. May 28 is Eid al-Adha (Bakrid), a national holiday that would normally see millions gathering for prayers, family meals, and community celebrations. The IMD has advised people to stay indoors during peak hours and stay hydrated — guidance that is difficult to follow for the millions who live without air conditioning or reliable electricity.

## The NRI Dimension

For the Indian diaspora planning summer visits home, the heatwave is a stark reminder of just how punishing Indian summers have become. What was once a manageable May heat has become genuinely dangerous, with conditions that rival the worst heat events anywhere on Earth. Several NRI families have reported delaying or canceling planned trips to North India, opting for monsoon months instead.

## What Happens Next

The IMD has forecast that the monsoon onset in Kerala — the traditional start of India's rainy season — may arrive between May 28 and June 3, slightly delayed from the normal June 1 arrival. Once the monsoon advances northward, it typically breaks the back of the heatwave cycle within a week.

Until then, India waits. The power grid strains. The death toll climbs. And for the hundreds of millions who cannot afford to stay cool, the next 48 hours will be the most dangerous of the year.
